Asheville, N. C., June 15,—An unexpected incident of President McKinley's visit developed yesterday afternoon, when it became known to newspaper men accompanying the party that permission to enter Biltmore house, George W. Vanderbilt's splendid mansion, had been refused to them, while extended to other members of the party. Mr. Vanderbilt is abroad and his representative, Charles Mc Nance, is with him. In the absence of both the estate is governed by L. J. Harding, said to be an Englishman by birth. Addison Porter, his secretary, was told of the incident. The state republican executive committee was called to order by Chairman F. H. R. Green at noon Tuesday as previously assigned.

Rev. Charles H. Strong preached the
third of his series of sermons on the sub-

tirely with the subject of evolution, and
the reconciliation of the teachings of sci-
ence with those of the gospel.

the creation, Rev. Mr. Strong said, than
that contained in the Apostles Creed.

earth." He referred to the many discov-

evolution have been traced out, and said
that there is now no antagonism between
those discoveries of science and that
statement of the creation contained in the
creed. There is no antagonism between
revelation and science, he said, as long as
each confines itself to its own department.
Evolution and revelation are separate and
specific subjects.

He spoke of the antagonism which has
existed between the discoveries of sci-
ence and the first chapter of Genesis, un-
til the literal interpretation of that first
chapter was abandoned. The question of
the order of development, however, was
a difficult one. In that, there does ex-
ist an antagonism between the discoveries
of science &c. and the first
chapter of Genesis. These discrepancies
puzzle until we refer to the definitions,
namely, that evolution deals specially in
the domain of processes, while revelation
deals specially in the domain of causes.
Genesis contains sufficient for our relig-
ion; the science of evolution sufficient for
our knowledge.

The teachings of evolution and its laws
could not have been unfolded to the men
of the day in which Genesis was writ-
ten. Their minds were not prepared for
the reception of such teachings. Rev.
Mr. Strong presented some points design-
ed to give a better understanding of the
meaning of evolution. It is the change
from the simpler to the more complex
form, he said. The trouble with many
writers on the subject was their indis-
criminate use of words which failed to
convey the intended meaning. Huxley,
for instance, was in the habit of using the
words cause, origin and genesis, when
they are things that man is unable to ex-
plain.

the theory of evolution, as applied to the
universe, to the earth, to the animal life
upon the earth and to man. Many, he
said, disliked to believe that man de-
scended from lower forms, but all the fos-
sil remains of prehistoric man gave un-
doubted evidence of this fact. In all forms
of life it is shown by science that there
is a regular graduation back to an original
type. Why should it not be so with re-
gard to man. The struggles of animal life
have been upward and onward to some-
thing better, something nobler, until at
last comes man, stupid at first but grad-
ually developing to what he is to-day,
with the hope of a still grander destiny
in the future.
